prompt:
Write an explanation of about 600 words of how a heat pump can heat a house when it is colder outside than inside. The reader is a homeowner deciding whether to replace a gas boiler.

Do not use parentheses.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.
sampling: harness defaults; not set by the experimenter
text:
A heat pump does not create heat by burning anything. It moves heat that already exists, and that single idea resolves the puzzle. Cold is a relative term. Air at minus 5 degrees Celsius still holds a large amount of thermal energy, because its molecules are still moving. Only at minus 273 degrees would there be nothing left to take. A heat pump collects some of that outdoor energy and delivers it inside your home.

The trick is a sealed loop of refrigerant, a fluid that boils at extremely low temperatures. In the outdoor unit, liquid refrigerant at well below freezing passes through a coil while a fan blows outside air across it. Because the refrigerant is colder than the air, heat flows into it and it boils into a gas. Heat always flows from warmer to cooler, so the refrigerant only needs to be colder than the air outside, not warmer than your house.

Next, a compressor squeezes that gas. Compressing a gas heats it, just as a bicycle pump warms up when you inflate a tyre. The gas can reach 60 or 70 degrees, which is now hotter than the water in your heating system. In a second heat exchanger, that heat passes into the water that feeds your radiators or underfloor pipes. Having given up its heat, the refrigerant condenses back to a liquid. It then passes through an expansion valve, where pressure drops and the temperature falls well below zero, and the cycle starts again. A fridge works the same way, only in reverse, pulling heat out of its cabinet and dumping it into your kitchen.

This is why heat pumps beat the arithmetic of a boiler. The electricity only runs the compressor and fans, while most of the heat is gathered from outside. A good installation delivers roughly three units of heat for every unit of electricity, a figure called the coefficient of performance. A gas boiler, even a modern condensing one, cannot exceed about 90 to 95 units of heat per 100 units of gas. Efficiency does fall as the weather gets colder, and modern units keep working down to around minus 15 degrees or lower.

Running cost depends on your tariffs. Electricity usually costs about three to four times as much per unit as gas, so at a coefficient of three the bills end up close to what you pay now, and lower if you use a heat pump tariff or solar panels. The carbon saving is larger, particularly as the grid gets cleaner.

What decides whether it works well for you is the house. Heat pumps are most efficient delivering water at 35 to 45 degrees, compared with 65 or more from a boiler, so they run longer at a gentler temperature. That suits well insulated homes with generous radiators or underfloor heating. In a draughty home with small radiators, you may need insulation work or some larger radiators first. You also need space outdoors for the unit, a hot water cylinder indoors, and a tolerance for a low hum from the fan.

Before deciding, ask two or three installers for a room by room heat loss calculation, not a rule of thumb. Ask for the predicted seasonal efficiency, the flow temperature they are designing for, and a running cost estimate using your actual tariff. Check what grants are available, since these can cut the upfront price substantially. If your boiler is nearing the end of its life and your home is reasonably insulated, a heat pump is a strong candidate. If not, fix the insulation first and revisit the decision.
